title: Whether Ellington ever took a stand on segregation
summary: Bigard says Duke never spoke out while he was with him, even though he called Jump for Joy a social statement, unlike Louis, who spoke up about Faubus.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Did Duke ever, to your knowledge, take any kind of a stand about segregated audiences or any kind of stand against segregated anything?

Well, not when I was with the band. To begin with, he didn't want to go down there anyhow. Now, that's where he and Louis was different. Louis, he didn't care about nothing because when Faubus was doing all that monkey business,
Louie said, he said, "Hey, you [illegible]," loud to everybody, and the world knew what Louie said. And he didn't care, I mean, Louie didn't care.
Well, Duke used to say that "Jump for Joy" was his social statement.

"Jump for Joy" was a beautiful show but if Duke had any kind of a backbone, because he was a powerful man, you know, and whatever he would say it could go a long, long way, see. But, no, he'd never say nothing.
I never knew him to, publicly --
-- and I just wondered if you ever --
had seen any instance of it. (Unintelligible.)
